=== 2026-10-07 SWG Briggs Brief to Issues 11 and 13 - Final.pdf ===
                             SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR          §                       BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY           §
LLC AND LCRA TSC TO AMEND           §                                     OF
THEIR CERTIFICATES OF               §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY           §                       ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST            §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL                  §
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE §
IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,   §
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,             §
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, §
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,    §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES             §

  SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

                                     I.     INTRODUCTION

       The Commission remanded two issues to this tribunal for supplemental briefing. See

SOAH Order No. 35, Item No. 6597. Both should be resolved against Applicants.

       On Issue 11, Applicants have not shown that the proposed Bell County East-to-Big Hill

765-kV transmission line is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. The SOAH

ALJs already found that “the record neither establishes independent need for Import Path 2 nor

that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030.” Proposal for Decision (“PFD”), Item No. 6441, at § VII.D.6.

The Commission’s prior approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) does not relieve

Applicants of their burden at the CCN stage to prove that this particular project satisfies the

statutory necessity standard under PURA § 37.056(a). See American Stewards of Liberty’s Reply

to Commission Staff and Applicants’ Exceptions to the PFD, Item No. 6537. That burden has not

been met.

       On Issue 13, the record fails to establish that the estimated congestion cost savings for

consumers justify the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project. Applicants’ congestion savings figures



SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                           1
 rest on the same overstated load forecasts that ERCOT itself has questioned, see PFD, and the

record contains no project-specific congestion cost savings analysis applying the System-Wide

Gross Load Cost methodology that ERCOT adopted in January 2025. See ERCOT, Congestion

Cost Savings Test Evaluation Guideline, Version 1.0 (Jan. 30, 2025). The ALJs should find that

Applicants have not carried their burden on either issue.

    II.       ISSUE 11: THE PROPOSED FACILITIES HAVE NOT BEEN SHOWN TO BE
              NECESSARY TO MEET STATE OR FEDERAL RELIABILITY STANDARDS

   A. Applicable Legal Standard

          The burden rests squarely on Applicants. The Commission “may approve an application

for a CCN only if the Commission finds that the CCN is necessary for the service, accommodation,

convenience, or safety of the public.” Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(a). Texas courts have long held that

PURA § 37.056 factors are to be evaluated in “the broadest possible terms.” Malone v. Pub. Util.

Comm’n of Tex., No. 03-11-00815-CV, 2013 WL 4820454 at *3 n.4 (Tex. App.—Austin Aug. 28,

2013, no pet.).

          Applicants bear the burden of affirmatively proving that this project clears the reliability

threshold; the PBRP’s prior approval does not substitute for that proof. Applicants’ own need

witness conceded the point: the Commission’s PBRP orders did not automatically grant a CCN,

and each proceeding must establish all PURA requirements. Tr. Vol. 2 at 42:9-19 (Gurley).

          Federal reliability standards under NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 require

planning assessments to demonstrate that the Bulk Electric System can withstand specified

contingency events without cascading, voltage instability, uncontrolled islanding, or thermal

overloads. Critically, those standards require the analysis to be based on credible load

projections—not speculative demand. Applicants’ witness acknowledged that ERCOT studied the




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                               2
 import paths together, in part because of TPL-001 contingency requirements, and that he knows of

no study that isolated this line on its own. Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:17-45:4 (Gurley).

   B. Argument

       Applicants have not demonstrated that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kV

transmission line is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. Four independent

grounds support this conclusion.

       First, the CCN proceeding requires independent proof of necessity—and the PBRP does

not supply it. Applicants will argue that the Commission’s prior approval of the PBRP settles the

reliability question. It does not. The CCN proceeding under PURA § 37.056 is an independent

adjudication in which Applicants must establish that their proposal satisfies the statutory

requirements. See American Stewards of Liberty’s Initial Closing Argument, Item No. 6225. HB

5066 directed ERCOT to develop a reliability plan, but “it does not dictate that any particular

infrastructure solution must be selected.” Id. The Commission’s PBRP Orders in Project No. 55718

authorized Applicants to file CCN applications; they did not pre-approve those applications or

foreclose the evidentiary inquiry at the CCN stage. See American Stewards of Liberty’s Motion to

Defer Need Determination, Item No. 5872. The hearing record confirms that Applicants offered

nothing beyond the PBRP and later ERCOT studies. Applicants’ witness testified that need “is

based on the Permian Basin Reliability Plan.” Tr. Vol. 2 at 208:13-15 (Martin). ERCOT (not

Applicants) performed the reliability studies, and no ERCOT witness testified. Tr. Vol. 4 at 49:4-9

(Gurley). Applicants did not analyze the necessity of the facilities themselves. Tr. Vol. 3 at 228:8-

11 (Gurley). Applicants’ need witnesses did not independently calculate the figures they sponsored

and could not explain how ERCOT built its models beyond what the report says. Tr. Vol. 4 at

49:15-50:10 (Gurley and Martin). Martin did not author ERCOT’s GTC exit-strategy study or run




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                              3
 its power-flow or contingency analyses. Id. at 39:21-40:8 (Martin). Staff’s witness likewise did no

independent study of need, no alternatives analysis, and no independent cost review. Tr. Vol. 3 at

274:1-18 (Poole). As the SOAH ALJs recognized in a companion docket, need remains a live issue

for determination in this proceeding. See SOAH Order No. 24, Dkt. No. 59182 (reserving need

issue for Docket No. 59475).

       Second, the ALJs have already found the record insufficient on need. The Proposal for

Decision in this docket concluded that “the record neither establishes independent need for Import

Path 2 nor that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030.” PFD at § VII.D.6. The record supports that

finding. Import Path 2 originated in the PBRP as part of the 2038 solution. Tr. Vol. 2 at 43:2-14

(Gurley). ERCOT’s December 12, 2024 sequencing letter states that only two of the three 765-kV

import paths are needed by 2030; Applicants’ witness conceded, “The words on the page say that

two of the three are needed.” Tr. Vol. 4 at 10:10-11 (Martin). The PFD further found that “the

record does not establish that Bell County East can supply power allegedly needed to flow west

into the Permian Basin.” PFD at § VII.D.5. These findings remain undisturbed. Staff’s witness

agreed that the real need is in West Texas, not in the study area, and that the project will not lower

costs for Bell County consumers. Tr. Vol. 3 at 253:19-254:2 (Poole). The remand for supplemental

briefing on Issue 11 does not reopen the evidentiary record. See SOAH Order No. 35, Item No.

6597 (“The Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) will not reopen the evidentiary record.”).

Applicants cannot now introduce new evidence to cure the deficiencies the ALJs identified.

       Third, changed circumstances have undermined the load forecasts on which the PBRP

relied. The PBRP was built on ERCOT’s 2024 load forecasts, which in turn relied on the S&P

Global 2022 Electrification of the Permian Basin study. See PFD at 78. Its forecast nearly doubles

from 12,240 MW in 2029 to 23,659 MW in 2030. Tr. Vol. 2 at 45:19-46:16 (Gurley). Applicants




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                               4
 did not verify those projections. Id. at 46:17-47:1 (Gurley). The load data underlying the

application were collected roughly two years before the hearing. Id. at 150:2-19 (Gurley, Martin).

Roughly 59% of the 11,695 MW of non-oil-and-gas load added to the plan was cryptocurrency

mining, id. at 144:1-10 (Gurley)—load that Applicants’ witness admitted has historically curtailed

during constraints, Tr. Vol. 4 at 45:12-16 (Martin). The planning forecast also included officer-

letter loads with no signed interconnection agreement. Tr. Vol. 2 at 148:1-149:1 (Martin). Since

the PBRP’s adoption, multiple material developments have eroded those projections: ERCOT

itself adjusted its load-forecasting methodology to reduce officer-letter-confirmed load and data

center load, as the PFD recognized. See PFD at § VII.C.1. Senate Bill 6 imposed credibility

standards for large load interconnections, requiring ERCOT to verify that projected loads are

supported by actual historical realization rates or other objective, credible, independent

information. Tex. S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025). Staff’s witness agreed that the load forecasting

underlying this application was built under the old methodology that SB 6 directed the

Commission to replace, and that reevaluation may be warranted as conditions change. Tr. Vol. 3 at

286:17-287:21 (Poole). ERCOT has publicly expressed “concerns with using the preliminary load

forecast values” for reliability analysis because many of the large-load projects submitted by

utilities may not materialize on time, at full scale, or at all. ERCOT, Preliminary Long-Term Load

Forecast for 2026–2032, Project No. 58777, Item No. 38; PFD at § VII.C.2. New planned and

announced gas generation in the Permian Basin has surged. As of 2026, there are 71 gigawatts of

gas generation in the development queue—compared to 22 GW when ERCOT completed the

PBRP in 2024—with 20 GW targeted for West Texas alone. See PFD at § VII.D.8 (“New Planned

and Announced Gas Generation in the Permian Basin”). Applicants’ witness acknowledged that

2,500 MW of Texas Energy Fund dispatchable generation is expected in Far West Texas, including




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                           5
 the 1,390 MW CPV Basin Ranch Energy Center by 2029. Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:18-42:5 (Martin). He

also conceded that the Far West reliability concern arises under nighttime, low-wind conditions

and stems from a localized generation deficit—insufficient generation near load. Tr. Vol. 3 at

213:12-214:8; 217:4-14 (Martin). This new generation, if built, would dramatically reduce or

eliminate the need for long-distance power imports via 765-kV lines. A reliability finding cannot

rest on load forecasts that the grid operator itself has questioned and that the Legislature, through

SB 6, required to be verified.

       Fourth, 31 members of the Texas House have called for denial. While legislative

correspondence is not binding authority, the joint letter from 31 House members urging the

Commission to “deny the applications for Certificates of Convenience and Necessity” for the

pending 765-kV projects reflects a significant legislative signal that the PBRP-based need case

remains contested and that the CCN process should not rubber-stamp prior administrative

approvals. See Item Nos. 6414 and 6444.

            III.    ISSUE 13: THE RECORD FAILS TO ESTABLISH ADEQUATE
                        CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FOR CONSUMERS

   A. Applicable Legal Standard

       Because the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project has not been shown to be necessary to

meet reliability standards (Issue 11), the project must satisfy the economic criteria under PURA §

37.056(d). That statute requires “a comparison of the estimated cost of the transmission project for

consumers and the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the

transmission project, considering both current and future expected congestion levels and the

transmission project’s ability to reduce those congestion levels.” Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(d).

       ERCOT adopted the System-Wide Gross Load Cost (“GLC”) Test as its method for the

congestion cost savings analysis. Energy and Environmental Economics (“E3”) recommended the



SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                              6
 test, and ERCOT codified it in the Congestion Cost Savings Test Evaluation Guideline. See E3,

Congestion Cost Savings Test for Economic Evaluation of Transmission Report (Mar. 2024); 16

Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i)(I). Under this method, a project meets the economic

criteria only if its levelized system-wide reduction in consumer energy costs equals or exceeds the

average of the first three years’ annual revenue requirement. ERCOT, Congestion Cost Savings

Test Evaluation Guideline, Version 1.0, § 2; see also Brent Bennett, Ph.D., An Economic

Assessment of the 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (Tex. Pub. Pol’y Found. 2026)

(“TPPF Assessment”) (savings must be “equal to or greater than the average of the first three years

annual revenue requirement”). Applicants bear the burden of showing that the project clears this

test.

    B. Argument

        Applicants have not carried their burden. The record contains no project-specific

congestion cost savings analysis for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project that satisfies the GLC

methodology. No witness isolated this line’s costs or benefits. Applicants’ need witness knows of

no study that evaluated this line independently, Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley); Applicants’

reliability witness offered no opinion on the cost of Import Path 2 and did not compare it to any

alternative, Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10-13 (Martin); and Staff performed no independent cost analysis, Tr.

Vol. 3 at 275:4-7 (Poole). Three fundamental flaws defeat any claim of congestion savings.

        First, the congestion savings projections rest on discredited load forecasts. Any congestion

cost savings estimate is only as reliable as the load forecasts underlying it. The PBRP’s congestion

analysis was built on ERCOT’s 2024 forecasts, which relied on the S&P Global 2022

Electrification of the Permian Basin study. See App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), att. JG-3; PFD at § VII.B;




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                             7
 see also Tr. Vol. 2 at 45:19-47:6 (Gurley) (2022 S&P forecast not verified). Those forecasts have

since been substantially undermined:

       ERCOT’s own preliminary Long-Term Load Forecast for 2026-2032 revealed that large-

load submissions from utilities exploded—Oncor alone jumped from approximately 5,018 MW in

2026 to roughly 109,554 MW by 2032—prompting ERCOT to warn the Commission that many

of the large-load projects submitted by utilities may not materialize on time, at full scale, or at all.

ERCOT, Preliminary Long-Term Load Forecast for 2026-2032, Project No. 58777, Item No. 38.

       Senate Bill 6 required ERCOT to verify that projected loads meet credibility standards

based on actual historical realization rates or other objective, credible, independent information.

Tex. S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025). No evidence in the record shows that the PBRP’s load

projections have been reconciled with these new statutory requirements.

       The PFD found that “the Far West Import GTCs do not cure the evidentiary deficiencies in

the forecasted loads.” PFD at § VII.D.4. If the load forecasts are overstated, the congestion

projections built on them are necessarily overstated as well.

       Second, the estimated lifetime costs dwarf any plausible congestion savings. The 765-kV

buildout carries an estimated capital cost of $13.77 billion for the three import paths, Item No. 67,

att. 5 (PBRP), and the total cost including local upgrades, financing, equity returns, maintenance,

and taxes has been estimated at nearly $100 billion over the projects’ lifetimes. See TPPF

Assessment at 1; PFD at 3; Tr. Vol. 4 at 209:25-210:4 (Poole) (cost-per-mile estimate rose roughly

21%, from about $6.2 million to about $7.5 million per mile). Staff’s cost estimates contain no line

item for steel and aluminum tariffs, which were set aside and not analyzed. Tr. Vol. 4 at 210:11-18

(Poole). And ratepayers will ultimately pay for the project. Id. at 192:20-23 (Poole); Tr. Vol. 3 at

253:19-254:2 (Poole). Even assuming the $400 million annual congestion benefit figure at face




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                                 8
 value—which is a system-wide figure not attributable to this project alone—it would take decades

to recoup even the capital cost, let alone the lifetime costs. And that figure measures the marginal

benefit of 765-kV over 345-kV, not the benefit over the status quo. The record simply does not

contain a credible showing that this project’s congestion savings justify its costs to consumers.

       Third, new gas generation could achieve congestion relief at far lower cost. The dramatic

surge in planned Permian Basin gas generation—71 GW now in the development queue versus 22

GW in 2024, with 20 GW targeted for West Texas alone, see PFD at § VII.D.8—represents a

market-driven alternative that would reduce congestion by siting generation closer to demand.

Applicants’ witnesses agreed that the PUC cannot dictate where generation is sited and that the

765-kV decision was made within a planning framework that assumes large interregional imports.

Tr. Vol. 2 at 69:14-17 (Gurley); Tr. Vol. 3 at 219:6-14 (Gurley). Staff’s witness agreed that

dispatchable gas generation in the Path 2 area could “potentially” be more cost-effective for

ratepayers than building Import Path 2. Tr. Vol. 3 at 262:11-21 (Poole). Applicants performed no

cost comparison between this import path and local generation. Tr. Vol. 4 at 42:23-43:2 (Martin).

Building generation where the load is, rather than importing power from hundreds of miles away,

is a fundamentally more cost-effective approach to congestion relief, and Applicants have not

shown otherwise.

                      IV.     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF

       For the reasons stated above, SWG Briggs I, L.P. respectfully requests that the ALJs find:

       On Issue 11, Applicants have not demonstrated that the proposed Bell County East-to-Big

Hill 765-kV transmission line is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. The

PBRP’s prior approval does not relieve Applicants of their independent burden under PURA §




SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.’S RESPONSE TO ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13                                               9
 37.056(a), and the ALJs’ own findings confirm that the record does not establish need for Import

Path 2.

          On Issue 13, the record fails to establish adequate estimated congestion cost savings for

consumers. Applicants have presented no project-specific congestion cost savings analysis under

the ERCOT-adopted GLC methodology, the underlying load forecasts have been discredited, and

the project’s estimated lifetime costs to ratepayers far exceed any plausible congestion savings.

          The ALJs should recommend that the Commission deny the Application, and grant such

other and further relief to which SWG Briggs I, L.P. may be justly entitled.

Date: October 7, 2026                                        Respectfully submitted,

            III.    ISSUE 13: THE RECORD FAILS TO ESTABLISH ADEQUATE
                        CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FOR CONSUMERS

   A. Applicable Legal Standard

       Because the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project has not been shown to be necessary to

meet reliability standards (Issue 11), the project must satisfy the economic criteria under PURA §

37.056(d). That statute requires "a comparison ofthe estimated cost ofthe transmission project for

consumers and the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the

transmission project, considering both current and future expected congestion levels and the

transmission project's ability to reduce those congestion levels." Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(d).

       ERCOT adopted the System-Wide Gross Load Cost ("GLC") Test as its method for the

congestion cost savings analysis. Energy and Environmental Economics ("E3") recommended the



SWG BRIGGS I, L.P.' s RESPONSE To IssuE Nos. 11 AND 13                                             6
 test , and ERCOT codified it in the Congestion Cost Savings Test Evaluation Guideline . See E3 ,

Congestion Cost Savings Test for Economic Evaluation of Transmission Report (Mar. 2024); 16

Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i)(I). Under this method, a project meets the economic

criteria only if its levelized system-wide reduction in consumer energy costs equals or exceeds the

average of the first three years' annual revenue requirement. ERCOT, Congestion Cost Savings

Test Evaluation Guideline , Version 1 . 0 , § 2 ; see also Brent Bennett , Ph . D ., An Economic

Assessment ofthe 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (Tex. Pub.PoVy Found. 1016)

("TPPF Assessment") (savings must be "equal to or greater than the average of the first three years

annual revenue requirement"). Applicants bear the burden of showing that the proj ect clears this

test.

    B. Argument

        Applicants have not carried their burden. The record contains no proj ect-specific

congestion cost savings analysis for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project that satisfies the GLC

methodology. No witness isolated this line's costs or benefits. Applicants' need witness knows of

no study that evaluated this line independently, Tr. Vol. 2 at 44:21-45:4 (Gurley); Applicants'

reliability witness offered no opinion on the cost of Import Path 2 and did not compare it to any

alternative, Tr. Vol. 4 at 41:10-13 (Martin); and Staff performed no independent cost analysis, Tr.

Vol. 3 at 275:4-7 (Poole). Three fundamental flaws defeat any claim of congestion savings.

        First, the congestion savings projections rest on discredited load forecasts. Any congestion

cost savings estimate is only as reliable as the load forecasts underlying it. The PBRP's congestion

analysis was built on ERCOT's 2024 forecasts, which relied on the S&P Global 2022

Electrification of the Permian Basin study. See App. Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), att. JG-3; PFD at § VII.B;

 see also Tr. Vol. 2 at 45:19-47:6 (Gurley) (2022 S&P forecast not verified). Those forecasts have

since been substantially undermined:

of the large-load proj ects submitted by utilities may not materialize on time, at full scale, or at all.

Tex. S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R. S. (2025). No evidence in the record shows that the PBRP's load

        Second, the estimated lifetime costs dwarf any plausible congestion savings. The 765-kV
